before.title: Tree-sitter for syntax
before.benefit: Multi-language structure without executing repository code.
before.tradeoff: Static syntax analysis has limits around dynamic dispatch and runtime call targets.

before.title: Graph, vectors, and GDS together
before.benefit: Neo4j supports relationships, semantic candidates, and community enrichment in one store.
before.tradeoff: Community clusters provide exploratory groupings rather than exact module boundaries.

before.title: Tools plus lazy source inspection
before.benefit: Question-specific observations and a separate source drawer keep bulk graph responses smaller.
before.tradeoff: Graph retrieval and source inspection serve separate workflows: the agent receives tool observations, while the reader can inspect code in the dashboard.

before.title: Bounded stages and batches
before.benefit: Limit active per-file work and write in finite transaction units.
before.tradeoff: Batch size and parser concurrency balance resource usage with indexing work.

after.title: Static syntax across languages
after.choice: Supported repositories span several languages. Tree-sitter extracts definitions and call syntax without running repository code.
after.benefit: One parsing pipeline supplies multi-language structure for exploration.
after.tradeoff: Syntax alone cannot resolve dynamic dispatch or runtime call targets.

after.title: Graph, vectors, and communities
after.choice: Repository questions need relationship queries and metadata-vector search. Neo4j stores both, with Leiden communities for an architectural overview.
after.benefit: One store supports relationship, semantic, and community views.
after.tradeoff: Communities are exploratory groups, not verified module boundaries.

before.title: Short transactions, explicit ownership
before.benefit: Claim and completion transactions keep task state and attempt history consistent while handlers run outside database locks.
before.tradeoff: Renewable leases protect ownership; handlers use destination idempotency when external effects must be deduplicated.
before.lesson: Design task-state consistency and external-effect safety together.

before.title: One durable authority
before.benefit: PostgreSQL coordinates admission, ownership, outcomes, and history in one place.
before.tradeoff: Polling and write contention make database pressure an important scaling consideration.
before.lesson: Use workload measurements to choose worker counts.

before.title: Priority and bounded attempts
before.benefit: Priority ordering supports urgent work, while attempt budgets bound repeated failures.
before.tradeoff: Fairness under sustained high-priority load remains a scheduling tradeoff.
before.lesson: Make scheduling and retry policy explicit.

after.title: Short transactions and renewable ownership
after.choice: Task state and attempt history must agree without holding locks through a handler. Use short claim/completion transactions and renewable task leases.
after.benefit: Task and attempt updates commit together while handler work runs outside transactions.
after.tradeoff: Database ownership does not deduplicate external effects; handlers need destination idempotency for those effects.

after.title: One PostgreSQL authority
after.choice: Admission, ownership, outcomes, and history share durable state. PostgreSQL is the authority; workers poll it for eligible tasks.
after.benefit: Database transactions coordinate independent workers and schedulers.
after.tradeoff: Polling and shared writes create database pressure as concurrency rises.

after.title: Priority with bounded attempts
after.choice: Urgent work and repeated failures need explicit scheduling limits. Claim by descending priority and cap each task’s total attempts.
after.benefit: Claim order favors higher-priority eligible tasks; the budget bounds retries and crash replacements.
after.tradeoff: Sustained high-priority load can delay lower-priority tasks; the policy does not guarantee fairness.
